content: Herpes simplex is a viral disease caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV), which exists in two main types: HSV-1 and HSV-2. Genital herpes is most commonly caused by HSV-2 and is typically transmitted through sexual contact. Oral herpes, often referred to as cold sores, is usually caused by HSV-1. Both types of the virus can cause episodes of active disease, characterized by painful blisters that contain infectious viral particles. These episodes typically last between 2 and 21 days and are followed by periods of remission when the sores heal. Most cases of genital herpes are asymptomatic, but viral shedding can still occur, meaning the virus can be transmitted even in the absence of visible symptoms. HSV-1 and HSV-2 are transmitted through direct contact with an infected sore or bodily fluid. After the initial infection, the virus migrates to sensory nerve cells, where it remains dormant for life. HSV-1 typically resides in the trigeminal ganglia, which provide sensation to the lips, lower mouth, and neck, while HSV-2 resides in the lumbosacral ganglia, which supply sensation to the genitals, perineum, and upper legs. Reactivation of the virus can occur, leading to recurrent outbreaks in the same area as the initial infection. Triggers for reactivation are not fully understood but may include factors such as sunburn, ultraviolet light, physical trauma, surgery, stress, or illness. Over time, the frequency of outbreaks tends to decrease as the immune system develops specific defenses against the virus. Anogenital Infection HSV-2 is highly prevalent, affecting approximately 25% of women and 20% of men in the United States. Among sexually active individuals with genital, anal, or perianal ulcers, genital herpes is the most common diagnosis, although syphilis is also a consideration. The prevalence of these conditions varies by geographic region and population. Ocular Infection Ocular herpes, primarily caused by HSV-1, is a specific form of facial herpes known as herpes keratitis. This condition begins with infection of the epithelial cells on the surface of the eye and can progress to involve the nerves serving the cornea. Herpes Encephalitis Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is a severe and potentially life-threatening infection of the central nervous system caused by HSV. It is one of the most serious viral infections affecting the human brain. Herpes Simplex Neonatorum Neonatal herpes is a rare but serious condition that typically results from vertical transmission of HSV from mother to newborn during childbirth. In some cases, the virus may be transmitted postnatally by a parent, caregiver, or sibling. The incidence of neonatal herpes ranges from 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 20,000 live births. Approximately 22% of pregnant women have been previously exposed to HSV-2, and an additional 2% or more acquire the virus during pregnancy. HSV-1 is increasingly responsible for genital herpes infections, particularly among young adults. Herpetic Whitlow Herpetic whitlow is a painful lesion on the finger or thumb caused by HSV. In children, the primary source of infection is often the orofacial region, with HSV-1 being the most common strain. This is typically due to finger-sucking or thumb-sucking behaviors. In adults, the primary source of infection is more commonly the genital region, with HSV-2 being predominant. Herpes Gladiatorum Herpes gladiatorum, also known as scrumpox or mat herpes, is caused by HSV-1 and is commonly seen in individuals who participate in contact sports like wrestling, rugby, or soccer. Abrasions in the skin provide an entry point for the virus. Recurrences may occur in the affected skin areas. Mollaret's Meningitis Mollaret's meningitis is a recurrent, benign, aseptic inflammation of the meninges caused by HSV. It is characterized by repeated episodes of meningitis symptoms, including headache, fever, and neck stiffness. Pathophysiology HSV-1 and HSV-2 can be shed from active sores or from apparently normal skin between outbreaks. HSV-2 is primarily transmitted through sexual contact with an infected individual, even if they are asymptomatic. HSV-1, while more commonly associated with oral infections, can also cause genital herpes through oral-genital or genital-genital contact. Genital HSV-1 outbreaks tend to recur less frequently than those caused by HSV-2. The most effective way to prevent transmission is to abstain from sexual contact or to maintain a mutually monogamous relationship with an uninfected partner. While condoms can reduce the risk of transmission, they do not provide complete protection, as the virus can infect areas not covered by the condom. Epidemiology and Demographics The prevalence of HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections varies globally. HSV-1 is more common in developing countries, where it is often acquired at a younger age, compared to industrialized nations. Socioeconomic factors, such as lower income and crowded living conditions, are associated with higher rates of HSV-1 infection. HSV-2 prevalence is lower in countries like the United States (20-30%), Australia (12%), the United Kingdom (4%), and Germany (14%). Risk factors for HSV-2 infection include being female, being Black, early sexual activity, having multiple sexual partners, and lower socioeconomic status. Asymptomatic Shedding Asymptomatic viral shedding occurs in most individuals infected with HSV, contributing to the transmission of the virus even in the absence of symptoms. Recurrence Recurrent genital herpes can cause painful sores, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems. Pregnant women are at increased risk of transmitting the virus to their baby, especially if they acquire the infection late in pregnancy. Cesarean delivery is often recommended for women with active genital herpes at the time of delivery. HSV infection also increases susceptibility to HIV, potentially playing a role in the spread of HIV. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis If untreated, herpes simplex infections can become recurrent. Neonatal herpes is a rapidly progressive condition that can lead to central nervous system (CNS) involvement and disseminated disease. Early symptoms include vesicular skin rashes, and without treatment, the infection can progress to CNS involvement, causing irritability, confusion, and respiratory difficulties. Disseminated disease can result in severe complications, including pneumonia, esophagitis, encephalitis, premature birth, spontaneous abortion, and infant death. Survivors may experience developmental delays or neurological deficits. Early treatment with antiviral medications like acyclovir improves outcomes, particularly in immunocompetent individuals. However, prognosis remains poor for immunocompromised patients and neonates with disseminated disease. Diagnosis Diagnosis of HSV infection involves a combination of clinical history, physical examination, and laboratory testing. Orofacial herpes typically presents as multiple, round, superficial oral ulcers, often accompanied by gingivitis and lymphadenopathy. Genital herpes can be more challenging to diagnose due to the absence of classical symptoms in many cases. Laboratory confirmation is essential for accurate diagnosis and management. Viral culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are the preferred methods for detecting HSV in lesions. PCR is particularly sensitive and is the test of choice for diagnosing CNS infections. Cytologic methods, such as Tzanck smears, are less reliable and should not be used for diagnosis. Treatment There is no cure for herpes simplex infections, but antiviral medications can reduce symptoms, shorten the duration of outbreaks, and decrease viral shedding. Oral antiviral drugs like acyclovir and valacyclovir are commonly used, while topical treatments such as docosanol can prevent viral entry into the skin. Daily suppressive therapy can reduce the frequency of outbreaks and the risk of transmission to partners. Experimental treatments, including natural remedies, may offer some benefit, but their efficacy is not well-established. A vaccine for HSV-2, known as Herpevac, has shown limited effectiveness in preventing infection in women but is not yet available for widespread use. Counseling A diagnosis of herpes can lead to emotional distress, including feelings of depression, fear of rejection, and social isolation. Support groups and online communities can provide valuable resources and emotional support for individuals living with herpes. Some individuals prefer to date others who are also HSV-positive to avoid the risk of transmission.
